abstract.para: This part describes potential problems when monitoring CPU temperatures and their solutions.

section.title: No sensors were detected
section.para: On laptops, the sensors-detect command may provide the following output:
section.screen: Sorry, no sensors were detected. Either your system has no sensors, or they are not supported, or they are connected to an I2C or SMBus adapter that is not supported. If you find out what chips are on your board, check https://hwmon.wiki.kernel.org/device_support_status for driver status.
section.para: This message is displayed when sensors-detect cannot find any hardware monitoring chips, which is common on laptops, where thermal management is typically handled through ACPI (Advanced Configuration and Power Interface) instead of a dedicated hardware monitoring chip.

note.title: The sensors command
note.para: Despite the message about the failure to detect sensors, the sensors command may still work and provide expected results.

section.para: You can check the CPU temperature directly from the ACPI thermal zone interface that the kernel exposes under the /sys file system, without installing any additional package. The CPU temperature is located in /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone*/temp. Below is an example of the command with its output:
The temperature is displayed in milliCelsius. To get the temperature in Celsius, divide the output by 1000 to get, in our example, 41°C.

note.title: ACPI may not be available on mainframes
note.para: Mainframes do not have the same power management needs as desktops, laptops and servers, and so they do not typically use ACPI. Instead, mainframes use different architectures and technologies for their configuration and management.

section.title: The displayed temperatures are unrealistic
section.para: If you suspect that the displayed temperature is too low or too high, you can try the following:

listitem.para: Check whether the sensors are detected correctly: Rerun the sensors-detect command to redetect the sensors.
Then, run the sensors command again to see if the temperature readings are more realistic.
Check the raw thermal data in the /sys/class/thermal/ directory. See whether the raw data matches the output of the sensors command.

Use a different tool to read the CPU temperature, for example, s-tui, a terminal-based utility that shows CPU temperature, frequency, and utilization in real time. It is available from Package Hub with community support.
Reboot the system to activate the change.
Then run s-tui from the terminal.

section.para: If none of these recommendations solves the issue, the problem might be due to unsupported or faulty hardware. In this case, you need to seek help from your hardware manufacturer.

section.title: The displayed temperature is too high
section.para: If the CPU temperature is too high, here are actions you can take:

listitem.para: Verify that the CPU cooling system, such as the fan or heat sink, works correctly. Ensure that the fan is spinning properly and that the heat sink is making proper contact with the CPU. If necessary, you may need to replace the thermal paste between the CPU and the heat sink to improve heat transfer.
Adjust the power settings on your system to reduce heat generation. Lowering the CPU frequency or enabling power-saving features can help keep the temperature in check.

Monitor the system load and CPU usage. High CPU usage for extended periods can lead to increased temperatures. Identify resource-intensive processes with tools such as top or ps, then consider optimizing or limiting their usage. For more information, refer to .
